176.title: The city of nine gates
176.hook: a stranger in a Varanasi lane asks Shankara which self should move aside, and the Gita explains the answer
176.carry: the same self sits in every body
176.howItsDone: Hindus greet with folded hands and namaste (literally 'I bow to you'), which many explain as a bow to the self or the divine in the other; in meditation, some draw attention inward from the senses, the 'gates' of Gita 5.13.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, two paths, renouncing and acting, and a lotus leaf that lives in the water without getting wet. Both reach the goal. Today, a city.
screen: `RENOUNCE OR ACT — BOTH REACH THE GOAL.`

segments.voice: Varanasi, on the river Ganga, more than a thousand years ago. The teacher Shankara is walking by the river with his students. In a narrow lane, a man comes the other way with four dogs: a man the society of that day treated as untouchable. Shankara tells him: move aside. The man doesn't move. He asks a question instead. Which should move away from which? This body, made of food, from that body, made of food? Or the self in me from the self in you, when it's the same self? Shankara stops. And he bows.
screen: `VARANASI, A NARROW LANE.` → `MOVE ASIDE, SOMEONE SAYS.` → `WHICH SELF SHOULD MOVE?`

segments.voice: That's a story told about Shankara; in many tellings the stranger was Shiva himself. Shankara answered in verse: whoever truly sees this, born outcaste or born a priest, is my teacher. The idea is the Gita's, chapter five. Verse thirteen: the one who lives in the body sits at ease in the city of nine gates. The nine gates are the body's openings: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, the mouth, and the two openings for waste. And who lives in the city? An old word-play hears purusha, the person, as the one who dwells in the pura, the city. Hindus call that dweller the atman: the self, the real you. Many teachers, Shankara among them, say it is one with Brahman, God in everything. The doing, verse fourteen says, is nature doing what nature does. Then verse eighteen, the verse the man in the lane was living: the wise look with the same eye at a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a person society shuns. Because the same one is seated in every city. It's why many Hindus greet with folded hands, namaste, I bow to you, and many explain it as a bow to the divine in you. Today it meets the people you look past: the person cleaning the office, the kid nobody sits with. The same self sits there.
screen: `THE STRANGER IN THE LANE.` · `NINE GATES: EYES, EARS, NOSTRILS, MOUTH…` · `THE ATMAN, SEATED WITHIN.` · `THE SAME EYE ON EVERY BEING.` · then, large: `THE SAME SELF IN EVERY BODY.`

segments.voice: Visit the gates one at a time: your eyes, noticing light; your ears, the nearest sound, then the farthest; your nostrils, the cool air coming in. You don't have to close any gate. Notice that something in the middle is noticing. Then bring to mind one person you passed today without really seeing, and silently, hands folded if you like, say namaste to the one seated in them.
Purusha. The person, the one who dwells in the city. Hindus call that dweller the atman, the self: seated at ease behind the nine gates, and the same in every body.

segments.voice: Carry this: the same self sits in every body. The same eye for the priest, the dog, and the man in the lane. See you tomorrow.

177.title: The peace that doesn't end
177.hook: Nachiketa turned down Death's gifts because they wouldn't last; chapter five names the peace that does
177.carry: lasting peace comes from the friend of all beings
177.tomorrow: Lift the self by the self
177.howItsDone: Hindu prayers and readings often close with 'om shanti shanti shanti', a threefold wish for peace, and some practitioners use steady, even breathing like that of Gita 5.27–28 to settle before meditation.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the city of nine gates, and the same self seated in every body. Today, the end of chapter five.
screen: `THE SAME SELF IN EVERY BODY.`

segments.voice: Remember Nachiketa, the boy at Death's door from day two? Death offered him gold, horses, a long life, music, anything, if only he'd drop his question. And the boy said: keep them. They won't last past tomorrow. Now think of the best meal of last month. Where is it now? Wonderful, and over by the end of the plate. The new phone, the great weekend, the compliment that made your whole Tuesday. Each one arrived, glowed, and left. The last verses of Gita chapter five ask Nachiketa's question: where's the happiness that doesn't end?
screen: `DEATH OFFERS GOLD.` → `KEEP IT. IT WON'T LAST.` → `A HAPPINESS WITH NO END?`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-two: the pleasures born of contact, of the senses touching their objects, are wombs of sorrow. They have a beginning and an end, and the wise don't take their delight in them. A womb is where something grows: every pleasure that depends on something outside carries, inside it, the sorrow of its ending. Nobody here says pleasure is evil. Verse twenty-three sets a practical test. Whoever can bear the rush of desire and anger here, in this life, is a yogi, a happy person. Not someone who never feels desire or anger. Someone who can bear the push of it. Verse twenty-four gives the other direction: happy within, delighting within, lit from within. That person reaches brahma-nirvana, the stillness of Brahman. Yes, nirvana: the word is in the Gita too. And the chapter's last verse names the source. The one who knows Krishna as the one who receives every offering, the great lord of all the worlds, and the friend of all beings, reaches peace. Shanti. That's a core Hindu teaching: lasting joy isn't something you collect; it's found within, in God, the friend of all beings. It's why so many Hindu prayers end om shanti, shanti, shanti. And it meets you in the quiet after something good ends, the trip, the show, the party. That ache isn't failure. It's the Gita pointing you where to look next.
screen: `WOMBS OF SORROW.` · `BEAR THE PUSH OF DESIRE AND ANGER.` · `LIT FROM WITHIN.` · `THE FRIEND OF ALL BEINGS.` · then, large: `SHANTI. PEACE.`

segments.voice: Sit tall and even out the breath, the way verses twenty-seven and twenty-eight describe, the air moving quietly in and out through the nostrils. If a want or an irritation pushes in, bear it for one breath and let it pass. Then, softly, out loud or under your breath, say what so many Hindu prayers end with: om shanti, shanti, shanti. If you don't pray, just say peace, three times, and listen to the quiet after.
Shanti. Peace: not the pleasure that begins and ends, but the peace of the one who knows the friend of all beings.
screen: `SHANTI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Carry this: lasting peace comes from the friend of all beings. The kind that doesn't end when the plate does. Chapter five, done.

178.title: Lift the self by the self
178.hook: Arjuna sank down in his chariot; chapter six says the self that sinks you can lift you
178.carry: lift the self by the self
178.tomorrow: A clean place, a firm seat
178.howItsDone: Gita 6.5 ('uddhared atmanatmanam', lift the self by the self) is often learned by heart, and some Hindus recite it as encouragement in hard times.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, shanti: the lasting peace comes from the friend of all beings that doesn't end, from the friend of all beings. Today, chapter six, the chapter of meditation, and a friend much closer to home.
screen: `SHANTI — LASTING PEACE COMES FROM THE FRIEND OF ALL BEINGS THAT DOESN'T END.`

segments.voice: Go back to the very start of the Gita. Two armies face each other. Arjuna, a great archer, looks across and sees his teachers, his cousins, his grandfather. His bow slips from his hand. He sinks down onto the seat of his chariot and says he won't fight. Everything Krishna teaches after that is an answer to that sinking. Now listen to the voice in your own head after something goes wrong. You always do this. What's wrong with you. Words you'd never say to a friend. Chapter six has two lines about that voice too.
screen: `HIS BOW SLIPS FROM HIS HAND.` → `HE SINKS DOWN IN THE CHARIOT.` → `WHAT DOES YOUR OWN VOICE SAY?`

segments.voice: First, Krishna clears something up. The true renouncer, verse one says, isn't the one who stops lighting the sacred fire or stops working. It's the one who does what needs doing without leaning on the fruit. For someone climbing toward yoga, verse three adds, action is the way up; for someone who has arrived, stillness. Then verses five and six. Lift yourself by yourself; don't let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self. In Sanskrit the same word, atman, the self, comes again and again, like a mirror facing a mirror. The word for friend is bandhu: a friend, and also kin. Here's the Hindu teaching under it. You are not your worst moment. Many teachers read the verse as the higher self lifting the lower, the steady mind lifting the scattered one. The verse doesn't say wait to be rescued, and it doesn't say you're alone; later chapters speak of grace. It says the lifting starts with your own hand. Then a portrait of the one who has done it: steady in cold and heat, praise and blame. A lump of earth, a stone and gold look alike to them. So when the inner voice piles on after you slip, the Gita's question is simple: which self is talking, the one sinking you, or the one lifting you?
screen: `THE TRUE RENOUNCER STILL ACTS.` · `LIFT YOURSELF BY YOURSELF.` · `THE SELF: FRIEND OR ENEMY.` · `YOU ARE NOT YOUR WORST MOMENT.` · then, large: `LIFT THE SELF BY THE SELF.`

segments.voice: Say the first words of verse five softly, out loud: uddhared atmanatmanam. Lift the self by the self. Now think of the last time the inner voice was harsh with you, and let the words come up. Imagine a good friend heard them said about you, and let the friend's answer come, warm. Say the line once more, and let that be the voice that answers.
Bandhu. Friend, kin: the self is its own bandhu. Gita six, five: the self is the friend of the self, and the enemy of the self. The lifting starts with your own hand.
screen: `BANDHU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: lift the self by the self. The harsh voice doesn't get the last word. Day one hundred seventy-eight.

179.title: A clean place, a firm seat
179.hook: on a battlefield, Krishna gives meditation instructions exact enough to follow tonight: the place, the seat, the mind on God
179.carry: a clean place, a firm seat, the mind on God
179.tomorrow: The lamp in a windless place
179.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep a clean corner or home shrine for daily sitting, often on a mat or cloth, with a straight spine and a steady gaze, following the pattern of Gita 6.10–6.17.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, lift the self by the self. Today, where and how to sit.
screen: `LIFT THE SELF BY THE SELF.`

segments.voice: A strange setting for a meditation class: two armies, conch shells blown, and a warrior who has just said he can't fight. And right there, Krishna gives Arjuna instructions so exact you could follow them tonight. Not vague ones. Where to sit. What to sit on. How high. How to hold your head. Where to put your eyes. And then a line that surprises people: how much to eat and sleep.
screen: `TWO ARMIES. CONCH SHELLS.` → `A MEDITATION CLASS.` → `WHERE, WHAT, HOW HIGH.`

segments.voice: Verse ten starts with the place. The yogi should sit alone, somewhere apart, with body and mind under control, not grasping. Verse eleven: in a clean place, set a firm seat, not too high and not too low. In the old instructions it's layered: sacred kusha grass, a deerskin, cloth. For most people now, a folded blanket or a steady chair. Verse twelve: sitting there, make the mind one-pointed and practice yoga to purify yourself. Verse thirteen, the posture: body, head and neck in a straight line, still and steady, the gaze toward the tip of the nose, not looking around. And verse fourteen, the heart of it: calm, without fear, the mind held, sitting with the mind on Krishna, intent on him. That's the Hindu teaching here. Meditation, dhyana, isn't only a calm-down trick. It's yoga, joining the mind to God, and the place is part of it. It's why so many Hindu homes keep a clean corner or a small shrine set apart, and why people take off their shoes before they sit there. Then the balance. Yoga, verse sixteen says, isn't for someone who eats too much or not at all, who sleeps too much or stays awake too long. Moderate in food and rest, in effort, in sleep: then yoga destroys sorrow. Today, look at your room. A bed, a desk, a charger. Is there one spot kept only for this?
screen: `A CLEAN PLACE, A FIRM SEAT.` · `BODY, HEAD, NECK IN A LINE.` · `THE MIND ON GOD.` · `NOT TOO MUCH, NOT TOO LITTLE.` · then, large: `A PLACE SET APART.`

segments.voice: Find the steadiest seat near you, a chair or a folded blanket on the floor, not too high and not too low, and let body, head and neck line up, as if a thread lifts the top of your head. Lower and soften the eyes toward the tip of the nose, stop looking around, and stay still. You can hold Krishna in mind, as verse fourteen says, or, if that isn't your way, hold the stillness itself.
Asana. The seat, and the way of sitting. The Gita's instructions: a clean place, a firm seat, body and head and neck in a line, the mind on God, and moderation in food and sleep.
screen: `ASANA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Carry this: a clean place, a firm seat, the mind on God. Not too high, not too low, not too much. See you tomorrow.

180.title: The lamp in a windless place
180.hook: the Gita's picture of a settled mind is a flame that doesn't flicker
180.carry: the settled mind: a lamp out of the wind
180.howItsDone: Hindus often light a lamp (diya) at the home shrine morning or evening, and some meditate by gazing at a steady flame; Gita 6.19's windless lamp is a classic image of the settled mind.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, asana: a clean place, a firm seat, the mind on God. Today, what happens once you're sitting there.
screen: `ASANA — A CLEAN PLACE, A FIRM SEAT.`

segments.voice: Light a small oil lamp, a diya, the kind lit at a home shrine, and set it by an open window. Watch it. The flame bends, leans, jumps, nearly goes out, flares back. Every breath of air pushes it around. Now carry it into an inner room and shut the door. The flame straightens. It stands tall and still, so still it almost looks painted. Same lamp. Same oil. The only difference is the wind. The Gita, chapter six, uses that picture for the mind.
screen: `A LAMP BY AN OPEN WINDOW.` → `SHUT THE DOOR.` → `THE FLAME STANDS STILL.`

segments.voice: Verse nineteen: as a lamp in a windless place does not flicker, that is the picture of the yogi whose mind is held, practicing union with the self. The Sanskrit is simple: dipa, the lamp; nivata, where there's no wind. Notice the lamp is still burning. A settled mind hasn't gone out. It's fully lit, just not being pushed around. That's the Hindu teaching of yoga in one picture: not an empty mind, a steady one, resting in the self. Then the verses say what that stillness opens onto. Where the mind comes to rest, seeing the self by the self, a person is content in the self. They know a joy beyond the senses, and once settled there, even heavy sorrow doesn't shake them. Then a definition I like a lot, from verse twenty-three: yoga is the unhooking from union with sorrow. Yoga is often heard as joining. Here it's also an unjoining. Now the practical part. Verse twenty-five: little by little, let the mind grow still. Shanaih shanaih: slowly, slowly. And verse twenty-six gives the method in one sentence: wherever the restless mind wanders off, draw it back from there and bring it under the self. Not never wandering. Coming back. Your day is an open window: every buzz, every tab, a gust. You won't stop the wind. Notice the lean, and shut the door again.

181.title: The mind is restless
181.hook: after all the instructions, Arjuna says what everyone is thinking, and Krishna agrees with him
181.carry: practice and letting go: abhyasa and vairagya
181.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often pair abhyasa (steady practice) and vairagya (detachment) as the two supports of meditation; the Yoga Sutra names the same pair, and some practitioners return to Gita 6.34–35 when meditation feels impossible.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, dipa: the lamp in a windless place, and the mind brought back, slowly, slowly. Today, someone admits how hard that is.
screen: `DIPA — A LAMP OUT OF THE WIND.`

segments.voice: You sit down to be still. Ten seconds in, you're thinking about lunch. Then an email. Then a conversation from 2014 that you lost, and how you should have answered. Then lunch again. Krishna has just described the yogi who sees the self in every being, and the lamp that doesn't flicker. And Arjuna, a warrior whose whole craft is a steady aim, stops him and says, basically: I can't do this. My mind won't hold still.
screen: `TEN SECONDS IN: LUNCH.` → `THEN A CONVERSATION FROM 2014.` → `ARJUNA: I CAN'T DO THIS.`

segments.voice: First, the vision that sets Arjuna off. The yogi, verse twenty-nine says, sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self. Whoever sees Krishna everywhere and everything in him is never lost to him, and he is never lost to them. And the highest yogi, verse thirty-two, looks at another's joy or pain as if it were their own. Beautiful. And Arjuna says: this yoga of evenness you describe, I don't see how it can last, because the mind is restless. Verse thirty-four: the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, strong and stubborn. To hold it, I think, is as hard as holding the wind. Here's the surprise: Krishna doesn't argue. No doubt, he says, the mind is restless and hard to hold. Then he gives two words. By abhyasa and by vairagya, it can be held. Abhyasa: practice, doing it again and again. Vairagya: detachment, the fading of the pull, not letting every passing want drag you off. You need both. Practice alone becomes grim effort against a mind that keeps being yanked away. Detachment alone never builds the habit. Together they work like two oars. Verse thirty-six closes it: yoga is hard for the one who doesn't hold themselves, but for the one who keeps striving by the right means, it can be reached. That pair, practice and letting go, became one of the best-known teachings in Hindu spiritual life. The mind is restless. True. And not the end of the story.
screen: `THE SELF IN ALL BEINGS.` · `AS HARD AS HOLDING THE WIND.` · `KRISHNA AGREES.` · `PRACTICE AND DETACHMENT.` · then, large: `TWO OARS.`

segments.voice: Rest on one thing, the breath at the nose, and come back to it each time the mind runs off, as it will. Notice where it ran; don't chase the thought or argue with it, just let the pull fade a little. Pull on both oars: return, and let go.

Abhyasa. Practice, repeated effort, paired with vairagya, letting go. Arjuna's honest complaint, Gita six, thirty-four: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn. Krishna agrees: by practice and letting go it can be held.
screen: `ABHYASA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Carry this: practice and letting go, abhyasa and vairagya. Every wandering is one more stroke of the oar. That's one hundred eighty-one.

182.title: The one who fell short
182.hook: Arjuna asks the question under every new habit: what if I start, and fail?
182.carry: no good effort is lost, even across lifetimes
182.howItsDone: Gita 6.40 is often quoted by Hindu teachers to encourage people who have lapsed in practice; some commentators divide the Gita into three sets of six chapters, and chapter six closes the first.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, abhyasa and vairagya: Arjuna admitted the mind is restless, Krishna agreed, and gave two oars, practice and letting go. Today, the end of the week, and the end of chapter six.
screen: `ABHYASA AND VAIRAGYA.`

segments.voice: What about the person who starts with real faith, and can't keep it up? The mind wanders off, and they never get there. Do they lose both worlds? Are they like a small cloud, torn off from the big one, that just thins out and disappears? That's Arjuna's question, the one anyone asks on day nine of a new habit. Six days, six big asks: the same self in every body; the peace that doesn't end; lift the self by the self; a clean place, a firm seat; the lamp out of the wind; the restless mind. That's a lot to live up to.
screen: `WHAT IF I START, AND FAIL?` → `A CLOUD, TORN OFF AND GONE?` → `A WEEK TO LIVE UP TO.`

segments.voice: A painful picture: you left the ordinary life, didn't reach the spiritual one, and now you're neither. Krishna's answer is gentle. Verse forty: there is no destruction for them, Arjuna, neither here nor in the next world. No one who does good, my friend, ever comes to a bad end. The word he uses there, tata, is tender, the way an elder speaks to a child. Then he tells what happens. The one who fell short reaches the worlds of the good, and stays long. Then they're born again into a good and prosperous home, or, rarer, into a family of wise yogis. There, verse forty-three says, they get back the understanding they had before, and they strive again, harder. Verse forty-four: they're carried forward by their earlier practice, even without meaning to be. This is the Hindu teaching of karma and rebirth at its gentlest: what you practice leaves a mark on you, and the mark travels with you. Every sit, every returned thought, every day of practice counts, and it carries. So the broken streak doesn't erase the days you kept. Through many lifetimes of effort, the yogi comes to the goal. The chapter ends by lifting the yogi above ascetics, scholars and ritual-doers, and saying that of all yogis, the one who turns to Krishna with faith, the inner self absorbed in him, is the closest. Nothing is lost.
screen: `THE TORN CLOUD.` · `NO ONE WHO DOES GOOD IS LOST.` · `THEY PICK UP WHERE THEY LEFT OFF.` · `EARLIER PRACTICE CARRIES THEM.` · then, large: `NOTHING IS LOST.`

segments.voice: Look back over this week, or this whole path so far, to a day you skipped or a sit that was all wandering, and instead of counting it against yourself, picture it the way verse forty-four does: as momentum. Every minute you did sit is still moving you. Breathe in and feel it carrying you; breathe out and let the missed days go.
Tata. My dear: the tender word Krishna uses for Arjuna. Gita six, forty: the one who strives and doesn't arrive isn't lost; earlier practice carries them forward.
screen: `TATA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: no good effort is lost, even across lifetimes. What you practiced is still moving you. That's chapter six, finished.
